utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Ierace, you're on your feet, and we expected something from the Prosecution by the end of this week. Please tell us what you've got to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, indeed I'm on my feet in relation to the issue of ABiH orders. I anticipate that by the end of today, I will be able to serve upon the Defence copies of documents which are the result of the search which has been undertaken over the last two weeks. Those documents are due to come into the possession of the trial team by 5.00 this afternoon. So it may be that if we do not get them until that point, that they are not delivered to the Defence until Monday. Although we are not obliged to deliver copies of the documents to the Defence, we are content to do so. The Rules only require inspection. Mr. President, in any event, I will be able today to provide the Defence with the results of 30 per cent of that search. The search has been undertaken of the 50.000 approximately documents which the Defence has told us they are anxious to have. The search of 30 per cent of those 50.000 documents has yielded 226 documents that may be relevant. Certainly, some of those 226 documents are relevant. The search was done by way of a search for key words or letters, and the 226 documents which are the product of 30 per cent of that body of documents is the end result. There is an index of those 226 documents which comprises some eight pages. The documents have not been translated. They are in the original language, Bosnian language, but there is a brief summary of the contents in the English language, often just a sentence or two, and that is included in the index. It is apparent that some of those documents are not material, for reasons such as they relate to a period of time outside the indictment period, they are of an administrative nature, or they relate to the 1st Corps but not to units that are deployed within the geographic area of Sarajevo. Nevertheless, we think it appropriate, given the stage of proceedings, that all of those documents should be provided to the Defence. Some of the documents are not provided in their entirety. For instance, there may be simply some pages within a document which relate to Sarajevo or the 1st Corps, in which case, those pages are provided. Some other documents refer to logs which are some hundreds of pages in length. However, should the Defence wish to have a full copy of those documents, they will be provided. The Prosecution will, of course, continue to search through material as it comes into our possession, through whatever trial team, which falls within our obligations under Rule 66(B). Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is there an observation you'd like to make at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I would like to thank my learned friend for the quality of his presentation and to add, because we can bring a comment at this point, in a few days, Mr. President, it was possible for the Prosecution to make a research on about 5.000 pages, or it was about 17.000 documents that they went through, 17.000 pages, approximately, they examined, and I must say that this was done very quickly. I must also say that the Prosecution could have done it much sooner, much earlier, and they would have been able to communicate to us this information which would enable us to cross-examine the witnesses, namely, in relation to some incidents that are more important. Therefore, the objections that we had said at the time today are even more serious since we needed a lot of time and we need lots of time to examine these documents. And as I said yesterday, we can always find time but we can never invent time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I should add that indeed these documents had been searched by the OTP, the Office of the Prosecution, in relation to the Galic trial, some months ago. The reason that we now produce further documentation is because we now possess a more sophisticated software search programme than we then had. You will appreciate, Mr. President, that to search for the 1st Corps amongst a myriad of documents is difficult because whether one searches the Roman numeral "I" or the normal "1," one has very severe restrictions in being able to sensibly sift through documentation. The more recent software enables us to do that, and we have only been in possession of that software since shortly after the trial commenced. And that has enabled us in this second sift-through this material to collect more documents, some of which will be relevant and some of which beyond that may be relevant. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The Defence deems that justice, with a capital "J," must not depend in any way of electrons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the ideal situation. On the other hand, you could also approach it from a different way and say that if the software helps us to do something that we couldn't perform before, that it assists the course of justice. I assume that the Defence will now, at least, looks at what the Prosecution has produced. I even can imagine that if there are any suggestions from the Defence side as far as the keys are concerned that have been used during the search, that this could assist the Prosecution in its ongoing effort to trace whatever documents that might be material to the Defence. I think it's not very wise to speculate on what that could result in, but I expect both parties to take the most constructive and positive approach in order to see whether the achievement until now could even be improved. Mr. Ierace, I think, then, we are now at the point where you can call your next witness, and that would be Mr. Gavranovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Stamp will take that witness. Might I be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please lead the witness into the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gavranovic, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I took it already from your answer that you could understand me. Mr. Gavranovic, before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this solemn declaration will be handed out to you now by the usher. May I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Witness answered through interpreter].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranovic, the order in this Court is you'll first be examined by the party who called you, that's counsel for the Prosecution. You'll then be examined by counsel for the Defence, and if there are any additional questions from the Bench, you'll hear from us. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. 1 1 Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your name Nedim Gavranovic?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993, did you also live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I wish to take you to the period of early 1993. Can you remember in what part of Sarajevo you lived?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What part of Sarajevo is that?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: In Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live in any particular part of Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Dobrinja III.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, at that time, there was a conflict going on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in respect to the -- before I put it that way, and there were lines of separation between the two parties to the conflict, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe for us where you lived in respect to that line of separation?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived very close to the separation line. It was a neighbourhood where, on the one hand side of the buildings, you had the members of the Serbian army, whereas across the road, in the other apartment buildings, there was the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you live?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in a building, in the next building, the building right behind the separation line, not far from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you lived on the side of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall the morning of the 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of day was that in terms of the weather?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a beautiful, sunny day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Twelve years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometime in the morning of that day, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to the football match that was being held not far from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say where this football match was being held?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: The football match took place on the parking lot not far from my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how far was this parking lot from your building?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Some 100 to 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, did you live with your parents?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were they willing or unwilling to allow you to go out of the house to the football game?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they didn't let me go right away, but I insisted to go. And then they let me go afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how did you come to know about this football game?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I had heard it from my friends who received this information. They had heard about this game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it to be one game or a tournament comprising many games that was expected to take place?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was a tournament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was the time and location of the tournament well known in the community before?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, some men knew about it. It was not broadcasted but people were talking about it. So people were able to hear about the game.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time did you arrive at the parking lot?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was morning, in the morning, maybe 9.30, 10.00, approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived, had the games started?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to when you arrived? Did you go anywhere in particular at that parking lot?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I first stood on the side closer to a building, and then I went and I stood behind a goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were watching the game, did anything happen?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: While I was watching the game, one shell landed, and then a second one landed as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say where the first shell landed?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: The first shell landed directly somewhere around the centre of the parking lot where the game was held.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just clarify that. Did this first shell land in the centre of the parking lot or in the centre of the football pitch where the game was being played?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It landed in the centre of the pitch where the football game was played.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And about how long after the first shell landed did the second shell land?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe 5 to 10 seconds after. Not longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the first shell landed, did you see anything or hear anything? Tell us what happened after it landed.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: At first, I wasn't aware of what was going on. I heard a very strong detonation; and afterwards, I felt the shock wave from the detonation because it had almost moved me a little bit. I turned towards the cars that were overturned behind my back. And afterwards, a second shell landed, and I started to run away. While I was running away, I was able to see people that were wounded. Some were unconscious, lying there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you run to?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I ran towards the closest street. And while I was running, I felt that there was something wrong with my leg. And when I arrived to that street, I saw my brother, who brought me to the closest car, and this is -- and they escorted me to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you the only injured person who was taken to the hospital in that car?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there other injured persons, I take it, injured by the shelling?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, to which hospital were you taken?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I was taken to the hospital in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened there? Were you treated there?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was conscious, I was sitting down at first and I was waiting for the people, the staff members, to give some assistance to the people who were heavily wounded first, because the hospital was full of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, describe to us, what was happening inside the hospital when you were waiting?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: They were bringing the wounded. Some of the wounded were transferred immediately to the city hospital in Kosevo, and they gave some assistance to some other people immediately right there. In the hospital, I saw lots of people that I knew. Some of them were unconscious. Some were lying down. Some were crying for help from the injuries. They were in pain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to you? What type of injury did you suffer?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I had an entry and exit wound on my right lower leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that injury was caused by what, can you say?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: By a shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the car park to watch the football game, about how many spectators were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: There were about 150 to 200 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the character of the crowd? Were there males, females, children, and men in the crowd?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly there were children and men, a few women, but not many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any persons in uniform in the crowd?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: There were some people in uniform, but they were fewer in number, the people in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what proportion of the crowd would you say was comprised of people in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but maybe 20 to 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody with any weapons there that morning?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the vicinity of that parking lot and in those apartment buildings of that parking lot, had you ever seen any military activity, any mortars, any soldiers armed, operating from there?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time, before you were injured, did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to school in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: In the basement premises that were turned into classrooms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that in relation to where you lived?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: They were buildings in the same block in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you wanted to leave your building to get supplies, for example, water or food, how did you travel?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: We had to pass along a lot of spots that were exposed to sniper Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fire, and it was very risky.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sniper fire was coming from where?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: It was coming from the area of Dobrinja IV, where the Serb army was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say who these snipers fired at?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: They would fire at whoever was passing by: women, children, adults. It didn't matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you lived through those circumstances and you lived through the war. Can you say -- tell us whether or not you have any long-term psychological condition as a result of the sniping at civilians?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I do feel some disorder. For instance, if I hear a loud noise, I get terribly scared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You went to the parking lot on the morning of the 1st of June, 1993, and there was a crowd there. Can you recall if there had been any other shelling that morning before the first two shells fell in the vicinity of where the football game was being held?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, there was no shooting to be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "no shooting," you mean no shooting apart from those two shells?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say the first shell fell in the middle of the place where the fellows were playing football?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On a general matter, living in Dobrinja in the course of this conflict, had you ever been anywhere in any situation where shells fell nearby?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And sometimes when shells fall, do you hear anything, sometimes?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometimes you hear the whistle of the shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the examination-in-chief, if it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Ms. Pilipovic, I see that you're standing. Is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness? Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Ms. Pilipovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavranovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This morning during the examination-in-chief, you told us about the incident that occurred on the 1st of June, 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that on the 30th of August, 2002 [Realtime transcript read in error "13th"] you spoke to the investigators of the Tribunal and made a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 30th of August in which year? I think that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the translation says that the statement would have been given on the 13th of August, 2002. Living in the future is still beyond human possibility. I don't know whether it's a translation mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the 30th of August, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 30th. So there are two mistakes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranovic, do you remember making that statement?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember making a statement. I don't know whether it was exactly on that date. I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence can show the witness the statement with his signature, for him to confirm whether that is indeed his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavranovic. Mr. Gavranovic, you told us today that you lived in the immediate vicinity of the separation lines. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that there was one building in which the soldiers were, that is, members of the army of Republika Srpska, and another building across the road where soldiers of the ABiH were.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether those soldiers lived in those buildings?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I think they did not. They lived in the neighbourhood, but they defended the neighbourhood there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you would see those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in passing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The buildings to which those soldiers went to their positions, were other people living in those buildings?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Not in that one building that was right on the separation line. No one was living there. People had moved out of that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how those soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: In camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I ask you how they were dressed, I'm referring to the period of 1992, 1993, and 1994. You were then young, but as far as you can remember, would you say that in that period, too, you always saw them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you see them carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that your building was a hundred or 150 metres away from the building which was on the front line. Can you tell us whether in your own building there were any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean whether they were living there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, who were living in the building and who from positions in your building defended the territory.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were people living in my building, but as far as -- I do not know of anyone shooting from that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any sniper positions on the lines held by Bosnian forces?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to show you a part of your statement that you made on the 30th of August --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I should like to read out just two lines from that statement of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, for the Prosecution, just indicate the page we are approximately on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 2 of the statement, fifth paragraph, last line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you state: "I assume that Bosnian soldiers close to our building had several sniper positions, but I don't know where those were."

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I may have said that, but that is not for sure. I said I wasn't sure whether they had any or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you're not sure where their positions were, if any?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: If any? I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period of 1992, 1993, and 1994, were you in a position to see and hear that there was shooting in the area of town that you lived in?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When I say that there was shooting, I mean cross-fire, shooting from both sides.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I just heard the sound of shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me how frequently you would hear that fire?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, almost every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in view of your age at the time, what weapons were being fired from in your opinion in most cases?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Mostly from rifles; heavy weapons also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that on the 1st of June, you were watching the match.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether before that incident, that is, before the 1st of June, 1993, were there any such similar group events on that location?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any shells falling on that parking lot prior to the 1st of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I think they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the duration of the war, not every day but occasionally. I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the consequences were? Do you have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't think anyone was wounded on that parking lot before this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that after the shells fell on this part of the parking lot, as you have told us, did any authorised officials appear on the scene of the accident - I'm referring to the police - to make investigations?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that 1st of June, you told us that you were wounded and that you were driven to the hospital in Dobrinja. Could you tell us the name of the hospital in Dobrinja, if it had any name?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Everyone called it the hospital in Dobrinja. It's not really a hospital but just some premises that some doctors turned into an improvised hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in hospital after that for 12 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you lie in that hospital? Were you in bed?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you had your medical documents when you were admitted and when you were discharged from hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many people were killed on that critical day?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number of dead, but I think about 15. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many were wounded?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that exactly either, but I think between 50 and 70. Something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the hospital in Dobrinja was called the military hospital?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day when you were at the match, do you know whether in the buildings that surrounded the parking lot -- and we know that those buildings formed the Cyrillic letter "P." Do you know whether there were any soldiers in those buildings?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they lived there, but as far as I know, they just lived there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that in your statement on page 2, said: "I assume there were soldiers in the building because it was customary for that area to be defended from apartment buildings."

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were not those buildings. Those buildings were about one block away from the first front lines, about 200 metres away. Maybe I meant those buildings, that there were soldiers in them. Yes, on the first lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were living in that building at the time, did you ever go to the front line?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether in the part of Dobrinja you lived in there were atomic shelters?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who used those shelters during the war?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, I think that the soldiers slept in those atomic shelters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in relation to the parking lot where this incident occurred, in your estimate, how far are the atomic shelters from that parking lot, either one or several of them?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe about a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us today during the examination-in-chief that you went to school and that instruction took place in the basement of the buildings in which you lived.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, and do you know, who was using the school?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: The school was destroyed because it was on the separation line, and no one could go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say it was destroyed, could you tell us when it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was destroyed repeatedly throughout the war because it was on the separation line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that since the school was on the separation line, that the BH army had positions in that school?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether any member of your family was a member of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate family?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any members of your family. Did you have soldiers who went to the lines?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the soldiers had their meals?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Probably in canteens, military canteens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "military canteens," did you have occasion to see where those military canteens in Dobrinja were?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said today in answer to a question from my learned friend, how many people there were in uniform, you said 20 to 30 per cent. That's what you said. 20 to 30 per cent were not?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I meant 20 to 30 per cent were in uniform, in my opinion, but that was a long time ago so I can't be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, those people who were watching the match and who were in uniform, did you know how old they were? Did you know them, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I knew most of them the people at the match. I can't remember exactly who was in uniform. But approximately the people in uniform were between 20 and 40 years of age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the first shell fell, did you see that very moment, and where were you?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it. I was just behind one of the goals, so that was about -- I don't know how I can explain that. On this parking lot, a part of it was being used as a football pitch, a smaller part. And I was next to the overturned cars which were to stop the balls from going over and from which -- so that they couldn't be seen from Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said there were cars, I think you said so that this part could not be seen from Serb territory. From what part of Serb territory was it possible to see that a match was being played?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No, you couldn't see that a match was being played. But if a ball was to go to the other part of the parking lot from which it could be seen. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the area in between those three buildings - so please correct me if I'm wrong - which part was open and from where could one see that a game was being played?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that open area, unprotected area, could be seen from the Mojmilo hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any troops at Mojmilo and which troops were there?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that at the very beginning, it was the Yugoslav People's Army, and later on, I don't know. I don't think there were any troops there, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, have you heard, that they were saying that on Mojmilo there was the positions of the army of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how old were the players?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, approximately from 18 to maybe 20, 25, 26, 30. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question put to you by my learned friend, you said that you were an eyewitness or that you witnessed shellings often.

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "frequently," what do you mean exactly? How frequent was it?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Personally, yourself, can you tell us what were the shellings that you witnessed and what were the consequences of those shellings and when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I often saw shells fall. In most cases, there was nobody around on the street. Nobody was injured in most cases. But there were also cases where people would be injured and sometimes one or two people would be killed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know if in that part of the city - and I'm talking about Dobrinja - if there were fightings taking place, if fighting was taking place between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, may it please you, Mr. President, except that I would ask for your respectful permission to ask one or two questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any specific reason why you kept them until now or just -- ?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No specific reason, but having regard to something which was asked in cross-examination, I thought that the information -- the witness might be able to provide some information to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp. Re-examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were approximately 200 spectators at the football game. Was it a noisy crowd?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: About 200 spectators, from what I was able to evaluate. I don't know. That day, it all looked normal. I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the crowd have been heard from the Serb part of Dobrinja, do you know?

utterances.speaker: NEDIM GAVRANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you all, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this question raise any additional questions from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gavranovic, since the Bench has no additional questions to you, this ends your testimony in this Court. We are all aware that it's quite a journey to testify for less than an hour in this Court, but nevertheless be convinced that it is important for this Court and it's important for the parties that all questions put to those who were present at the relevant places and relevant times are important for us because they give information which might assist us in preparing the decisions we'll have to take. So thank you very much for coming to The Hague, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps before we continue, Mr. Stamp, has the exact spot of the 360-degrees photograph of yesterday resulted in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have not located the person who took those photographs to give us that precise information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we are asking if perhaps we could be allowed to supply that information in the forthcoming week. I think we might be able to give the GPS reading, as well as the exact spot as it is related to other places that was described by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then wait for a while and see whether the objection stands or not. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. I am surprised, I am astonished, that with so many technical devices and this, I would really like to do -- General Galic is really astonished as well, and I am absolutely astonished that we cannot find out where the picture was taken from so that the Defence may act consequently. I think that this is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'll just ask you a question. You objected yesterday. Are you willing to wait until the information you asked for is there, or do you want us to take a decision and not to wait any more? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would ask you to take a decision now on this matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If a decision is to be taken now, I would respectfully submit to the Court that the whole essence of what the witness has said is that this -- the photograph that was shown to the Court is an accurate and fair depiction of the area surrounding where the incident occurred. He could describe the apartments; he could describe the hills in the distance, the water tower, the whole surroundings and environs of the car park. So it does, from the evidence before the Court, gives the Court a useful depiction of the area in issue, and it has been identified by the witness as accurate. And if that is so, it is of some use in determining certain of the issues which are before the Court. And therefore, it is admissible. The issue as to whatever weight a photograph of that nature will furnish to the Court or can be used by the Court is something else which we could come to later on. But as far as whether or not it is admissible, from what the witness has said, it does, it is respectfully submitted, show the Court quite accurately the environs where the shelling incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I submit that that is sufficient in the circumstances, in the circumstances of a shelling incident where there were two shells fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's the position of the Prosecution that even if you would not have on the position of 10 or 15 or 20 or 30 metres the exact location from where the photographs were taken, that they nevertheless might have probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And therefore are admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if I could add one thing: We will be in a position to provide the exact position in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. President. There is a reason for which we maintain this position. The reason is the following: The witness that we heard yesterday stated that he was standing at approximately a metre fifty from the impact point of this shell. It seems that technically and, unfortunately, it is almost impossible to survive such a detonation, such an explosion, that would have occurred at a metre fifty from somebody that would have taken on a hard surface such as an asphalt surface. We shall try to prove this later. But it is highly improbable that this witness could have been situated at a metre fifty from such an explosion of an 80 millimeters mortar. It is quite impossible. So I would like to know if the picture was taken from one extremity of the pitch or the other. The witness stated, I believe it was an expression, but he said that he had received approximately 1.500 shrapnels in his body, and we are quite astonished by this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation of the basis of your objection, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Stamp, your next witness will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Omer Hadziabzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text of this declaration will be given to you now by the usher, and I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Later, you'll be examined by counsel for the Defence. So that's the order in this Court. And if we have any additional questions, we'll put them to you as well. Mr. Stamp, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Examined by Mr. Stamp:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your name.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: My name is Omer Hadziabdic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For about how long have you lived there?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Since my birth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm terribly sorry for Mr. Stamp, for interrupting him. I must interrupt for the clarity of the debate. If I understand correctly from the French booth, the questions asked by Mr. Stamp were inaudible. Mr. Stamp would maybe like to repeat those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that the -- we have an English translation, but if the interpreters were not able in the French booth to translate them, I would rather suggest that we repeat what is on our transcript. So I'll -- could we first have a confirmation of the French booth that they are not able to hear Mr. Stamp, and not to hear the answers? I now have to switch to five. Could you confirm? Thank you. I will then slowly repeat what the questions and the answers were so that the French booth will be able to translate it so that we don't have to go through the questions, at least, we don't have to put them to the witness again. The first question was: "Could you please tell us your name." Answer: "My name is Omer Hadziabdic." "And do you live in Sarajevo?" "Yes." "For about how long have you lived there?" "Since my birth." Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you live there in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which area or community in Sarajevo did you live in 1993?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: In 1993, I lived in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say what part of Dobrinja you lived at?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Dobrinja III. Dobrinja IIIB.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you recall the years 1993 and 1994? Did you experience any sniping or shelling in the community where you lived?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the nature of the sniping first.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Throughout 1993 and 1992, and a large portion of 1994, we were submitted to sniping fire, shelling. The sniping fire with regards to the building where I lived was accessible from all sides. So the sniper shot from both sides, from one side and through the other side through the street. So the sniping fire was dividing the street in two. Therefore, it was impossible to go from one building to the other. And the same thing happened between my heating plant and my building, we couldn't go through because of the sniping shots. And we also had to go to the woods to get wood. We did not have any wood. We did not have any heating because the heating plant was shelled. It was not operational, and this is why we had to go to the woods to get the wood, and we were always submitted to sniping fire. So every time that we would try to go for water, to gather wood to heat, any humanitarian movement, any humanitarian reason that we had to move, everything we had to do to survive was hindered and our lives were always at stake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who these snipers targeted or shot while you lived in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No, they did not choose their targets. They shot, they fired independently of the age, independently also of the fact whether it's a civilian or a soldier, an adult or a child. They did not look at the ethnicity. They didn't choose their target. They shot at everything that moved, even animals. They didn't even choose between an animal and a man. They shot at everything that they could at.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These snipers that you speak of who shot at both civilians and soldiers, from where did they fire?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: They fired from the positions held by the Serbs, positions held by the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us about your experience in relation to shelling in that period.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Shelling took place on a daily basis. They were shelling targets according to their own choice. It was not important to them whether it was a civilian target or a military target. They were just firing at targets independently of whether they were civilians or military targets. I, myself, was a victim of a shell. I was myself injured or wounded by one of the -- by a shrapnel coming from a shell. I talked about the heating plant earlier. It was shelled as well, although it is not a military target. My building was also shelled, although it is not a military target. The shell fell on our building. With regards to the street, the same thing was happening on the street. The park, also, where children played. This park was for children to play there, and for them, that represented also a target. They shelled the park. They shelled every place they wanted. They did not choose their target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that even when people were involved in humanitarian activity such as collecting water, they were the victims of sniper fire. Can you remember where you would go to collect water?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: We would go for water, if you're talking about drinking water, first we had to go to Dobrinja V to get it. And from my building, the place where we would go to get water was approximately 500 metres away. I'm not quite sure. Then we dug up a well, but the capacity of this well was not sufficient to supply all of us with water, so we would have to wait for a day or two for the water to come from the well, because the quantities were quite limited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you go a little bit more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you'd have to wait for a day or two for water to come for the well -- from the well. Where was this well?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: The well was behind the building across the street from my building. This is where we had dug up a well, and there was a hand pump that was placed there. It's a sort of a old-fashioned hand pump that you can see in villages. And this is where we would get water, but the water was only sufficient for drinking water. We didn't have more water than that to use. We could only cook that water or drink that water, whereas the water to wash ourselves, to wash the clothes, for that kind of water, we would use the water from the stream. But in order to get to that stream, we had to go on two occasions --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that stream called?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It's called Dobrinja stream. This is how we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in order to get there, how would you travel?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: There were visual shelters from sniping activities. We had to go first through a space between buildings. My street was cut off, if you will, from the sniping activities. And as you go towards the stream, you had to go across that sniping field. This is how we called it. We said we had to go over that one sniper, where that one sniper was firing, and then visually they had -- we had built a barrier so that the sniping -- sniper doesn't see us. But if the sniper just decided to shoot, it couldn't really protect you from the fire. So after we passed that one sniper, we would go towards the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of barrier was that?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you built a visual barrier. Can you say what it was built of?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Those were -- on that part for which I'm talking now, those were overturned cars, old cars, that were placed there so that the sniper doesn't see if somebody runs across or that the sniper cannot see that person clearly so that the target cannot be very clear and precise. So the sniper was able maybe to see you, to see somebody run. But the sniper could not really pinpoint the exact position where the person was so that the sniper was not able to target the person running across. Then we would go towards the river. Now, near the river, the river was also covered by snipers. But under the bridge, we used -- see, the angle from which he was firing, if you go under the bridge, he doesn't see us well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Sure. So then the bridge was covering us. The bridge was covering us in a way, but it was difficult to get to that bridge. And so when we get to the bridge, there was a trench that was dug out, not very long trench, and then we go through the trench, and then we used that bridge as a cover, because he was probably shooting from somewhere up high. So he couldn't really see us very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of any persons who were shot in any of these areas? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I know of one person, but I don't know his name. I know he was shot at the stream when he went to fetch water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, can you say when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I think -- I think this was in 1993, though really I don't remember the dates very precisely, whether it was 1993 or 1994. All this was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am about to turn to a different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and since it is 10.30, that would be a suitable moment to have a break. Mr. Hadziabdic, we'll have a break for half an hour. That means that Mr. Stamp will resume his examination of you as a witness after that. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours, before I proceed, may I just make one quick submission. I just would like to submit respectfully that I don't think there would be any serious prejudice to any party if the decision as to the admittance of the 360-degree photograph be postponed until we can get more information before the Court, notwithstanding my earlier submission that in respect to a shelling incident where there is no direct line of sight as where the Prosecution say the thing is fired from, the precise spot is of no great moment, but perhaps the Court, if it sees that there's no prejudice to the proceedings, could postpone any decision until we could get that information for the Chamber's benefit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider that, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, could I take you now to the day, the 1st of June, 1993. On the morning of that day, what was the weather like?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It was a typical summer day, no rain, no clouds. So it was the normal summer weather.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you leave from your home to go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: That morning, I didn't go out at all, though I was meant to go. That was the first time I didn't go, because it was Bajram, and we observe Bajram by going to the mosque first thing in the morning, about 7.00 or 8.00. You go to the mosque. That morning we didn't go to the mosque because it was too risky because of sniping and other things. The mosque was located in a building in Dobrinja II which used to be an Alhos shop, a textile shop, before the war. That is where the mosque was, because the old mosque was destroyed. It was on the front line, so we didn't dare go to the mosque because of sniping. And that is why that morning I didn't go to the mosque. We didn't go anywhere. I stayed at home. Later --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Later, did you go anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Later, I went to the basement because I had nothing to keep me occupied. I couldn't go anywhere else but to the basement, because, you know, when there is Bajram, we have something sweet to eat, but we had nothing to eat, in fact. We didn't have sugar even to make tea, so this made me nervous, and I was upset, and I went downstairs to calm down, to do some repair work on my bike, simply to keep me occupied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: And since --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Remember to take it a little bit slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's also because of the translation. You speak rather quickly, and the interpreters have to interpret everything you said into English and to French, so I think that's the reason why Mr. Stamp urges you to take it a bit more slowly. I hope you understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the basement you went to is the basement of your apartment building?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. In my own, to my own cellar, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you worked on your bike there?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I was repairing my bike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you repair it?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I was able to in those days. Since the window of my cellar faces Dobrinja IV and Lukavica, that is, the direction I later learned when the tournament was organised, I heard some noise. In those days, when ten people were talking, that was a noise, because there were no cars driving around. There was no electricity, so you couldn't hear any noise at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, thank you very much. Now remember to take it slowly and to listen to what I'm asking. Having done some work on your bicycle, did you go anywhere after that?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that there were people, and there were some noise, and then I went out to try and test my bicycle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I went behind the building. Before the war, there was a kind of children's playground and a parking, lot, an area that was not covered by snipers. So at least as far as sniping was concerned, one could move around safely. And it was an exceptionally quiet day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this -- you spoke of a tournament. Did you go to that tournament?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was a football tournament?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. As this is close to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- well, I was about to ask where in relation to your apartment building was this football tournament taking place.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It was taking place behind my building, at the parking lot. So I tested my bike over a distance of some 100 metres, and then I went up to see what was going on. I still didn't know that there was a tournament, in fact. And as I approached, I saw -- I recognised many of my friends. But as I was on my bike, I couldn't get right up to my close friends because I couldn't reach them by bike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: So I found a spot for myself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, may I ask you the following: You're giving us a lot of information. Some information is more relevant than other information, and as you might have noticed, or perhaps you know - and if not, I'll inform you - that these trials take a very, very long time. And therefore, I would ask you to listen very carefully to Mr. Stamp and to answer specifically to what he asks you. If, for example, he were to ask you have you come to the Tribunal by car? Then you could answer, yes, I came by car, or I did not come by car. Whether the car you came in was red or blue or whether there are five or six or seven passengers, if Mr. Stamp would like to know that, he'll ask that in his next question. So he'll then ask you, was the car red or blue? But you're giving us a lot of information while we're trying to use our time very efficiently, and we want to get specific answers to specific questions. So could you please try to help us. Listen well, answer the question, and if there's any additional information we need, I'm certain that Mr. Stamp will ask you for that. This is no criticism; this is just explaining how we work in this courtroom and how we are trying to use our time as efficient as possible. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the parking lot, was the football game in progress?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I'm not sure what time it was, about 10.00, 10.30. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was a game being played at that time?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. It was in progress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where exactly in relation to where this game was being played did you go to?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: We were to stand in the middle of the pitch and facing the goal. I'm talking about the goal closer to where the shell fell. So it would mean the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I take it from your answer you stood near to the right-hand corner of the football playing area, if you are facing the direction where the shell came from, or the shell fell, I beg your pardon. And your answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. If you're standing in the middle of the pitch. I'm talking about the first shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, tell us: A shell landed on the pitch. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Correct. The pitch itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us what happened when that shell landed?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: The match was ongoing. I was standing where I said when the shell impacted. We heard a terrible explosion. There was black smoke in front of our eyes. I felt a very strong blow in my chest, and the explosion threw me over a car, and I fell. And instinctively, I covered my head, expecting a second one, expecting a second shell, because I knew that one was never enough.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as you lay there, did anything happen after that?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. Some people started running away in panic, those who could run, without thinking of the possibility of another one falling. Then shortly after that, a couple of seconds later, a second shell fell a few metres away from the first. And this second shell again affected quite a number of people and wounded them, those who were running away. So it was the same kind of explosion that was heard a couple of seconds later. And of course, the cries, the screams and panic. After that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One moment. You said twice that the second shell fell a couple of seconds later. Can you just tell us what you mean about how long after the first shell fell did the second one fall?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Maybe 10 or so seconds later. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the second shell fell, did you do anything?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. I got up. I felt my chest where I had felt the blow, and I thought the shrapnel had hit me there. Later, I did notice maybe a pebble or something had hit me. But anyway, nothing dangerous. I saw that nothing was wrong. There was no blood. And I started running. As I saw other people running away, I, too, ran to the closest entrance to the building, the closest building and one of the entrances that had been made there. It wasn't a normal entry place but an improvised entrance to that building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you reach to that entrance?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, I entered. I went inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what followed after that?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: When I got inside, I found a young man there. I later learned his name was Ferid Muzaci. He was wounded in the palm of his hand. He was bleeding profusely. Without knowing that I, too, had been wounded and seeing that he was bleeding heavily, I tried to help him. There was panic. People already knew where the shell had fallen, that there were a lot of wounded people. Some women came running down the steps, looking for pieces of cloth or anything to stop the bleeding. As there was no sanitary medical equipment available or bandages, ordinary cloths were used. And then I, myself, realised that something warm was flowing down my leg, down my left leg, was running down my leg. I saw a hole in my trousers, and my trousers were bloodied. I realised I, too, had been wounded, and the first thing that occurred to me was my mother, what she was thinking, because already people knew that a shell had landed. I left that guy to the women and I went looking for aid myself, and I wanted to get home, to let them know I was alive. And then I saw my mother running towards me in panic, looking for me, and I kept saying "I'm okay, I'm okay," and she saw me holding on to my leg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stop there. Were you taken to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which hospital was that?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I was taken to the Dobrinja hospital, which is maybe 5 minutes on foot, 5 to 10 minutes on foot from the spot where the shell had fallen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you treated there?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, they gave me first aid, that is, they just stopped the bleeding because there were many people with far more serious injuries and the hospital was too small to deal with them. So I was given first aid and left to wait until they hospitalised those who were in a worse condition. So I was there waiting for my turn to come to be treated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you admitted that day or were you discharged home?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I was discharged for treatment at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you return to the hospital from time to time for treatment?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. For dressing of my wounds and for regular checkups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, I'd like to show the witness document marked P2506B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Mr. Usher, could you assist Mr. Stamp. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Once again, a problem of translation. I see here that the translation is incomplete. What I suggest we do is that we wait for Mr. Stamp's questions, and then we will come back and we will have a request to make that we be shown the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I follow your suggestion that we first wait what questions Mr. Stamp will put to the witness. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have a look at that document which was given to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a copy of your medical report in respect to your treatment for the injuries you received from that shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, it's a copy of the report I received that same day in hospital, after which I was sent home, for treatment at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Firstly, do you see your name on the document?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. My surname and name, Hadziabdic Omer, and my year of birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that you got it the same day. We will get to that document that you have shortly. Do you see written in hand on it various dates going down to the 16th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you got it on the 1st of June, 1993, can you explain how it is that these writings were made on it?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I received the report on the 1st of June, 1993, when I was admitted to hospital and when I was treated. Then, you see, I was sent for home treatment, and it says, "Check-up in two days' time in the bandaging department." And then, by hand, there is an indication when I reported for check-ups, when I was bandaged and given medical treatment. All this went on until the 16th of June, 1993. So what is written here is when I was bandaged and when I should come again for a check-up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: On the 16th of June -- on the 16th of June, 1993, I was bandaged, and I was told to come back in four days' time. So it didn't end on the 16th. I reported once again four days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You took from your pocket a document. What document did you take from your pocket? Could you just tell us in two words what document that was?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It is the original of this document. This is the original of this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were at the football pitch immediately after the two shells fell, did you recognise any of the persons who were injured there?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, many of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were -- could you tell us the composition of the people who were killed and injured? Were they males, females, children, adults, older people?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Mainly, those were men. Most of them were civilians and children. So there were a lot of my friends of my age, and I, myself, was 15 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have spoken to the Court or you have told the Court about your experiences of sniping and shelling in that civilians in the Dobrinja area. Having lived through that, have you any long-term psychological effect or trauma as a result of the sniping and shelling of civilians in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Of course.
