What happens to a person at an early age can never be forgotten, especially if one loses one's dear friends, friends who were only guilty of being born or having been born, perhaps, in the wrong country at the wrong time; Young men born and killed because they were called Adil or they had some other name; young men who were not guilty of anything, who were perhaps of another ethnicity, and in the end, children who wanted to go outside and see something nice. They were killed for no reason, and you know very well that I, myself, was a victim of many sniping shots. It happened to me that I had to lie down in the snow for many hours because of the sniping activity. You know, these things cannot be forgotten so easily.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the conflict, were you able to identify any sound Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. coming from an arriving mortar?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. When you hear the sound, it means that it's already gone. It has already passed by. You cannot hear the noise, and then you see it. When you hear the noise, it's already gone. And that same thing would happen when you would deal with small calibre weapons, and even airplane bombs that had such fearful sounds that our blood would freeze in our veins. But we became so used to it and we became such experts in these sounds that we could recognise what kind of projectile was passing by when you hear that noise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of sound would a mortar make if it passed by and you heard it?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: "Bzzzt," something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not in a position to help the Court with a description. I think we all heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think if there would be any need --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you would have to hear it to understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be any need at a later stage to know exactly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the man who is laughing right now, if he had heard it, he would really not find it so funny, especially if he would have lost a dear friend after hearing that sound. I don't know what's so funny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the story you're telling is not funny. The sound you made, we have some difficulties --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The gentleman was laughing, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that being taken back to these moments might hurt you. Nevertheless, I have to ask you to refrain from comments because we're in a court of law here and we'll listen to everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's fully accepted. Mr. Stamp, I would say that it's very difficult to describe this sound. If there would be any need for anyone, we're in the lucky circumstances that we have an audiotape, so everyone could listen exactly to what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far did you live from the place where this football game was taking place?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Between 30 and 50 metres. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that location, were there any military positions in the location of your apartment building and the park itself, parking lot?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No, there were no military positions, not before, not during, and not after the match. So those were just apartment buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That, Mr. President, is the examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Hadziabdic, it's now up to counsel for the Defence to examine you. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You were treated, if I understood correctly, at the Dobrinja hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were you treated in a military hospital?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Because I couldn't go to the city. Only the heavily wounded people were able to get there over the barricades, and those barricades were hit, were targeted, by the gentlemen who were under the command of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am a bit late in rising and I will try not to rise every time something like this happens but I didn't hear any evidence from this witness that he was treated at a military hospital. Maybe I'm mistaken. My friend is putting it to the witness that that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Stamp, this stems from your own documents that you have submitted. This is a delirium. You must read them.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All I'm saying, is that it is improper to put to this witness that he stayed at a military hospital unless there's an evidentiary foundation for it. He may ask the witness, "Did you stay at a military hospital?" But the witness has not put that in evidence. But he ought not --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is very simple. This is a document that stems from the Prosecution, and they are pretending not to know what it means.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you kindly read what is written on that stamp that's at the middle of the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, let's try to make everything as clear as possible. The mere fact that documents of the Prosecution indicate that it was a military hospital does not mean that it is the Prosecution's view that the hospital was a military one. On the other hand, we usually accept, especially of course in cross-examination, questions to be leading. Mr. Stamp, when I look at the question put by Mr. Piletta-Zanin, at least in the English translation, it doesn't say that it was the witness who said that it was a military hospital. He said something like, if I understood well, understood from where is not specifically mentioned. If it would be in dispute, then of course we could ask Mr. Piletta-Zanin to rephrase his question. If it's not in dispute that it was a military hospital - I don't know whether it is or not - but then of course the witness could be led to the hospital as being a military one, and then asked why he went to such a hospital. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is my submission that is precisely the way the question was put to the witness, "Why were you treated in a military hospital?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To put a question like that, it would have first -- it would be proper to establish first that the witness understood himself to be treated in a military hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you that if there has been no discussion between the parties on whether Dobrinja hospital was a military hospital, it would have been proper for Mr. Piletta-Zanin not just to assume on the basis of documents provided by the Prosecution that it was a military hospital. If, for example, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you have presented in evidence several times annexes to the report of the committee of experts, if the Prosecution could take it from that that the committee of experts, the whole content of it, would be admitted as being true by the Defence, you might have a problem. So let's not assume just on the basis of facts contained in documents provided by the other party that these facts are not in dispute. So let's try to be a bit precise on that. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be very clear, Mr. President, as I try to be always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read what is written on the stamp in the middle of the page. No, Witness, please do not take that document. Please take the other document, because I haven't seen this particular document that you're holding. Would you kindly take the other document, whether you like it or not. Yes, that one --

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: This is the original. I can see it better.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is not my problem. I am asking you to take the document that I have seen, and not the document that I have not seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, there's one document I understand that you brought yourself, and the other one has been given to you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin now invites you to look at the document given to you in this courtroom. And you explained to us that it's the same, but would you please look at the copy given to you in this courtroom, which has a sticker on it on the top. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you kindly read only what is written on the sticker or the stamp right in the middle of that document.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I am terribly sorry, but would you like me to read what I see or what I know what is written?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do not want to know what you know but what you can see.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: We can read "V J N A B O D," it looks like an "O B," and the rest is illegible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You only read half of the word. I did not hear you read "Sarajevo," which is perfectly legible. So you either cooperate -- you do not see Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, I do see Sarajevo. I'm terribly sorry. I was only reading the upper portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, will you use your voice in a different way. Will you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the words that you have read, the letters that you have read, as we have seen it, for the first word, should we not consider it to be the word "Vojna"?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It can also be JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you treated by the JNA, by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if it is not the Yugoslav People's Army, would you then say that that first word would stand for "Vojna," "military" in translation?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You do not know or you wish not -- you choose not to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, the hospital in Dobrinja you were treated in, was that a military hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can see on the stamp "military hospital, Dobrinja," and on the upper hand corner, we can see "hospital of Dobrinja." I really don't know if this is a military hospital or a civilian hospital but I do know that all the wounded would go to that hospital to be treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you notice any military personnel, doctors, nurses, whatever, in that hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All the doctors were wearing outfits like all other doctors in the world. And like all the other doctors in every other hospital, they were all wearing white clothes. I didn't see anybody wearing a military outfit. All the doctors were wearing white clothes, which is a typical medical way of dressing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you have any other indication, apart from perhaps the documents you received, that it was a military hospital??

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot conclude from anything else whether it was a military hospital or a civilian hospital. I really do not know. I only know what I saw myself and what I see now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, but what I wanted to note as well, that in the English translation that we received bearing number B1, we do not see the mention of this military word, of this stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the witness, of course, we noticed that there's no translation of the stamp, and I expected of course you to come back to that. But perhaps we first not discuss the documents but first examine the witness and, at the end, we'll see what other observations are there to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you stated on page 11, line 12, that you had not seen any military activities inside the buildings that were around the parking lot. Do you confirm this, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: On that day, I did not see any military activities going on, not in my building and not in the two other buildings that surround the parking lot. I have not noticed anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, the days that preceded the incident, were there any military activities going on in your building, the building you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: In my building, there were no [Realtime transcript read in error "in"] military activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, not far from the football pitch, was there a front line with trenches?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, but on the other side and inside the hill, so on the other side of the road and on the hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at how many metres, please?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you precisely. Maybe a hundred metres, 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, is this what we call the first defence line?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: The first defence line was located 300 metres away in the building of Partizanska Olimpijada. It was the first building of the community Dobrinja IV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before continuing, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in the English transcript it reads on page 53, line 7: "In my building, there were in military activities." It was our understanding that the witness testified that there were no military activities. Just for sake of clarity. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I thank Judge Nieto-Navia for his observation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you're talking about the first front line situated at 300 metres away. Where was the second defence line?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I do not know. I was 15 years old at the time, and I'm not a military expert. I was not going in, going there, going on the defence line. I was not going to the first defence line. I did not go into the trench that you're talking about. I did not go to that line that was right in the hills. Children were not allowed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about Mojmilo hill, Mojmilo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. You have stated that you are not a military expert. However, earlier in your statement on page 31, line 6, you have indicated to us that "they," and we do not who you're talking about exactly, but they were targeting all targets independently of civilian targets or military targets. Since you were not an expert, Witness, what makes you say -- how can you know that there is a difference between a civilian target or a military target?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: You can decide for yourself. Is a child who is 13 or 15 years old a military target or not?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have stated they were shooting at anything independently of what it was, whether it was a military target or a civilian target, but could you tell us, Mr. Witness, where were the military targets? Those are your own words. So where were those military targets in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: A military target is a line, a mortar, a bunker, a military bunker. But a football pitch is not a military target where most spectators are children. That is not a military target. So when I told you, for instance, where the first line of defence was, that's a military target.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I asked you if you knew where the military targets were located, since you make a difference. For instance, do you know where the general headquarters were of the 5th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know in an approximate way, could you tell us, in a general way?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Dobrinja II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the street name?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it right next to the Dobrinja hospital?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it not at a distance of some 100 to 150 metres from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're saying that you don't know exactly, but could that have been the case?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Maybe yes, maybe no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you that everything is possible in life, but do you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know, Witness, where the atomic shelters are located, those that belonged to the Dobrinja buildings?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if near the football pitch was there an atomic shelter?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What distance was it from there?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Approximately 100 metres away. But the building was in between, and the building is still there, actually. It's right there in between the football pitch and the atomic shelter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was using this atomic shelter, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain if the mosque was there during the war. I can't tell you about it now because I'm not sure if it was there at the time. I'm not quite sure. I know that there is a mosque, but whether it was erected right after the war or during the war, I don't know. But that mosque is still there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know if inside these atomic shelters the military was stationed? Were there any soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: What do you mean "soldiers"? What do you mean, in what capacity are you talking about soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the military sense of the word. A military man is a man who is not necessarily armed, an armed man, because we know that not enough weapons were able for everybody. But military men are soldiers independently of the fact whether they carry a weapon or not. Soldiers.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Are you talking about soldiers on duty or soldiers while they are not on duty to take shelter inside the shelter, maybe to go to the mosque --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see, Witness, that you are testifying almost as an expert witness. That's very good. So do you know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Refrain from comments, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, and ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us, if you know, and answer with a yes or a no, do you know if soldiers were stationed in those atomic shelters?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you do not know or you choose not to say?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know for what period of time you're asking me this question. I don't know what kind of soldiers. Is it a soldier that went to the mosque not carrying a weapon or a soldier that is -- I don't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I will help you. I will help you. What can you tell us, regardless of the period of time, but during the war, what can you tell us about soldiers who would have been stationed or who would have gone to atomic shelters?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It is possible that there were some soldiers, but not on duty, not carrying out any kind of order. It was not a barracks. Maybe they were there to take shelter from something. That is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you said that there were no barracks there, but where were the barracks in Dobrinja located?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. If there were no barracks, where did the soldiers sleep?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: They were on the front lines. I don't know how they were structured but, anyway, those who were on the front line, they were on the front line. And those who were not on the front line were at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the soldiers, where were they quartered? Where did they sleep?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Probably on the front lines, those who were on assignment. So some would be on duty; others would be sleeping, and then they would take turns. And those who were not on the front line, they went home. They stayed with their family, wives, children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what were their weapons? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: You mean our whole army or the weapons at the disposal of our army or of the soldiers on the front line?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking but what you saw. Did you see soldiers coming back from the lines, armed with mortars? If you did, tell us. If you saw something else, tell us that, please.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I did not see soldiers armed with mortars. As for weapons like rifles and such like, that could rarely be seen because most of the weaponry was at the front. So the people changed but the weapons remained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know whether civilians manufactured their own weapons with, for instance, water pipes, any makeshift weapons?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Civilians, I don't know. I don't know about civilians making weapons out of water pipes. I never saw anything like that. And what I didn't see, I can't tell you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, it's better that way. Witness, to come back to what you saw, please, with regard to the apartment buildings, the buildings that were close to the front line, were they used by forces of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, when they went home to sleep with their families, wives and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were certain buildings used as positions for defence, as firing positions from which fire could come?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: The first line, that building was abandoned by the civilians. On the first line were the military positions. That is the first line, the first building next to Dobrinja IV, that is where the military was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in an apartment building, a building that was an apartment building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It used to be, but it was abandoned by the civilians. It was used by the army, so that was the first line. That line could have been destroyed and trenches built, but the building was used such as it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Where was the second line, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know much about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you localise it very approximately?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Probably at the trenches, up there at Mojmilo. I don't know for sure. But since this was an apartment building, it wasn't open space. There was no need to mark the second line. Then the second line would be where you would have to withdraw and take up positions when you're forced to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, do you know where the various headquarters of various battalions were?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Imagine, if children knew such things, what would be the purpose of military secrets?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but we know that children are intelligent and they know a lot of things and they hear things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this is my last warning as far as comments are concerned. You have to refrain from it, and I'll insist on that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first take the question. Mr. Hadziabdic, the question to you was whether you knew about various headquarters. Your answer was not a direct one. You said "if children would know about it..." Do you have any knowledge on where the headquarters of the various battalions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can just speculate about that. It would be guesswork. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. If you might know, even approximately, the locations of the battalions, could you tell that to this Chamber to assist us? Could you do that?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I assume in Dobrinja II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let me try and be a little more precise. We know that a brigade is divided up into battalions. Are you telling us that all the battalions had their various headquarters in Dobrinja II, or were there battalions that had headquarters in other locations or other parts of Dobrinja, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know where the areas of responsibilities of various battalions were and, therefore, where their commands were. I've already told you that I can only guess about it, so my guess is that it was in Dobrinja II. That is my guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer. Witness, are you aware of the existence of a tunnel which was dug under the airstrip of Dobrinja, under the runway?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you please, if you know, tell us, where was the entrance to this tunnel on the Dobrinja side?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: The entrance was in C5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "C5," what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: A part of the neighbourhood. Now, whether it is the airport settlement or Dobrinja, but anyway, it was a neighbourhood known among the population as C5.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you yourself see the entrance to this tunnel?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I never entered that tunnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether this tunnel was guarded by military forces?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Probably it was. Either the military police or the civilian police; I don't know. I'm not quite clear about that. But anyway it had to be guarded to make sure that people didn't enter it randomly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the military police, Witness. Do you know where the military police was located in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Probably in Dobrinja II.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, do you know the name of a person called Lucavic, I think, who was responsible for the military police?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I do know a director of Energopetrol, whose name is Edin Loncarevic. But he was director or Energopetrol and I know him as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Witness. This person, Loncarevic, therefore, was he in charge of the military police at the time in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: In what period of time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think 1992, 1993, up to 1993, even the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Possibly. I don't know. I don't know anything officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, whether there was any rivalry between the army on the one hand and the military police on the other?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Do you know, Witness, if the Territorial Defence was constituted in Dobrinja at the beginning of the war, that is, in the months of April and May, maybe June 1992? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Well, it was only normal for something to be organised because if there hadn't been some sort of defence, I wouldn't be here to testify now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, this defence, Territorial Defence, was it supplied with uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: At first. It depended on how each individual managed. But what is quite certain, they had insignia. They did have insignia. People knew whether they were soldiers or civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're telling me that members of the Territorial Defence were recognisable as soldiers. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: One could put it that way, that they were recognisable as soldiers because they had insignia, and it was known that they were soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they also carry weapons?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Who had weapons carried them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. So you're talking about insignia. Could you tell us what kind of insignia they were that -- by which they were recognised?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: TO. TO, and the Bosnian coat of arms with berets, and on the berets, they carried the coat of arms and the TO sign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you familiar with a sniper unit which operated on the side of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the berets that you mentioned a moment ago, were they green berets? Was the colour green?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: There were various colours. There were few of us with weapons. So one day they would wear red ones, the next day yellow ones, so as to give the impression that we were no -- more numerous so that they wouldn't attack us. That was the tactics applied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, regarding this football match, we understand that the people playing were between 18 and 26 years of age. From what age did the mobilisation order make it incumbent upon men to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Let me correct you first. Not necessarily between 18 and 26. Whoever knew how to play, played. When you choose a team, you just chose those who could play. As for people who had to respond to mobilization, it applied from 18 to 19. You had to go for training. I don't know exactly what the situation was that year. At first, it was only those who had served in the JNA that went while there were weapons. And as the need for more men arose, people were mobilised. So I don't know whether just then they mobilised people of 18, young men of 18. So I'm talking of the period of the month of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you, yourself -- are you hearing me?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I can hear you now, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you, yourself, ever carry weapons in Sarajevo, in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you, yourself, ever take part, offer any kind of assistance to the defenders, who were sometimes called "defenders of Dobrinja"?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question? I didn't understand it quite.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Did you in any way whatsoever, during the period we're interested in, provide any kind of assistance to those who were known as the defenders of Sarajevo, in this case, Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: No military assistance or anything else. No assistance, except for the normal assistance every human being would give another. But anyway, I wasn't asked to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you telling me that everyone in such a situation assisted the defenders of the city?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It depends what you mean by assistance. If my neighbour who is not on the front line, he is there, and I have salt and he needs some salt to make bread, of course I'll give him salt. Is that the kind of assistance you're referring to? If he's thirsty and I have water and I give him water, is that assistance? There was plenty of such assistance. But if you mean assistance in the sense of me charging his clips and helping him clean his rifle, I didn't provide any such assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to show the witness a document which we received from the Prosecution, which has not been translated, but I think there's no need for it to be translated. It is 0038-015. If I may do so with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can tell us -- you say there's no need for translation. I'd rather see whether the Chamber agrees with you. Could you tell us in the presence of the witness what the document is approximately about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a list which I can show you, Mr. President, of a certain number of patients who were admitted to Dobrinja, and we see the dates, the date 1st June, 1993, which needs no translation, names which don't need to be translated. Then initials "D" which I assume doesn't require translation. It stands for "Dobrinja." Then some numbers. Again -- and my question will relate to the numbers, which again need no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] D86, sure. [Interpretation] Has the witness got the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you find your name on that list? And for the assistance of the others, it is in the last third of the page, beginning of the last third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Hadziabdic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, next to your name, to the left, there's a date, and that is the 1st of June, 1993, is it not? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, let us go to the right of this document. Let us forgot the letter D, which is not of any use now, and let's go to the next column, the last column to the right. In the line where your name is, what do you find there, please? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, will you please look at the document that we read a moment ago given to you by the Prosecution; that is, P2506B, and the Serbian version of that document, please. Do you have this document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're now asking the witness questions about a document on which you indicated that you would submit to us objections. Of course, this confuses --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- because if you would object into the admission of evidence, then of course it might be difficult to ask him to use it during his testimony. Could you please clarify your position in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be glad to. The problem is the following, Mr. President: The numbers we have to the right are, in fact, numbers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that's a practical explanation why you're putting these questions to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm coming to it, Mr. President. We have, on the right, protocol numbers, and we see that the document shown by the Prosecution, there is no protocol number, apparently. So what I wanted to ask the witness was whether he, himself, can find this protocol number on this document. Because we find it quite astonishing that we are given documents with protocol numbers and without protocol numbers. So we would like this witness to confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine. But if you ask the witness to testify on the other document and at the same time you'd object against the document being admitted, what's, in your view, the way we should deal with the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The following way: I would like this witness to look at the document, and since he tells us that he has an original - he told us that following by a question from Mr. Stamp - let this witness tell us simply whether on that original we find the presence of this protocol number. I think it would be useful for everyone that we know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that you would like to have the original presented to this Chamber as well? Otherwise, we cannot check. And that, finally, that both the copy and the original will be part of the proceedings? Do I understand you correctly? I mean, I'm just wondering, if it would ever come to an appeals hearing and we have discussed at large and there's a lot of testimony about documents which are not there finally in the proceedings which will be presented to the Appeals Chamber, how would you then expect an Appeals Chamber to understand what happened in this courtroom? So it's a matter of procedural law rather than whether there's a good reason to ask questions. I do not object against that. But I'd rather like to know what finally will be admitted, what will finally be exhibits in this case, or not, specifically in view of these medical documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what I wanted to do was the following: I can say this in front of the witness. As he has the original before him, and without tendering it necessarily, that the witness look at the original and read for us the protocol number that may be on it. And if he doesn't see that protocol number, he will simply tell us that he doesn't find that protocol number. And I think that is the clearest way of doing it. And we will see then how to proceed. If I may be allowed to ask this witness to read on his original the protocol number, if he can find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll first ask Mr. Stamp what's the position of the Prosecution in this respect. Because until now, when a document was not tendered in evidence, that was because both parties agreed on the content. And this was usually text. Text can be read out, and if everyone agrees that the text on the document is read out, it's irrelevant whether -- what kind of characters these were. It's about the text. And here it seems to be about the content of a document as a whole. Could you please, Mr. Stamp, give the position of the Prosecution in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would submit that the document which is not intended to be received in evidence should not be used in this way in terms of the entirety of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Perhaps what my friend could inquire of the witness is whether or not the copy which we intend to tender to the Court is identical to the original which he has brought. And then the witness could refer to the copy which we propose to tender to the Court. It would achieve what I think my friend is trying to achieve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just confer for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This Chamber would first like to know at this very moment, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, exactly your objection against the document tendered by the Prosecution, since that's 2506B. You said you would make a submission later. We would invite you to make it now and to tell us whether it's still the wish of the Defence to have the original available as well because that was indicated before the witness showed us that he had a document brought with him. Could you please, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I could not do this before the witness. I believe that we could maybe do it later, for purely practical reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Then I'll suggest that we would have to have a break anyhow. That the witness perhaps starts already with his break. Mr. Hadziabdic, we have a legal technical issue to be discussed. So we'll perhaps do it when you're not there because it might influence you one way or the other. So I'll ask you to leave the courtroom, guided out by the usher. But I've one additional question to you. I noticed, at least you said that you had the original document with you. Would you be willing to give the original to the Court? Of course -- well, not at this very moment. But would you be willing to, if it would assist the Court for the proceedings to have the original in our possession? Thank you very much for your willingness. You'll hear after the break whether we'll need it or not. Mr. Usher, could you please lead Mr. Hadziabdic out of the courtroom. And we'll resume at, presumably, approximately 1.00. Might be 5 minutes later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In fact, what I wanted to do in order to submit to you these difficulties would have been to submit certain documents to the witness, but since I will show these documents to the witness later, however, you wanted me to talk to you now, I will then submit these documents now. So I propose to show you these documents so that you, the Chamber, may know what it is all about. These are excerpts and they refer to the hospital Dobrinja and to see if -- the authenticity of these documents. So with your leave, I would like to show you these documents now so that you may see what we are talking about. May I have your permission? Even if these documents are not admitted at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are these documents known to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are documents that we wished to distribute. We have a sufficient number of documents for everybody, but they stem from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you indicate, as I requested you yesterday, to the Prosecution that you would use them?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet, Mr. President. Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I asked the Defence yesterday to do --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what kind of documents they are using. So we'll not have a look at them at this very moment. Perhaps you could do it after the break. But you first should show it to the Prosecution and to make clear to them what kind of documents you're going to use. But my question was about a different matter. My question was about to give the objections against the document used -- to be tendered -- at least we expect to be tendered by the Prosecution. That's Exhibit 2506B. What we noticed by now is that the stamp has not been translated. I saw some other small parts. For example, under the address, there are a few words missed which are not translated. I see that the date is 16.93, which is translated as 1 June, 1993. I see a few differences. But apart from the translation, or perhaps aspects of the translation we have not noticed yet, are there other objections against the admission in evidence of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The objections are not about the date, because even if it's a typo, because we see 1.6.1993, I think everything understood that it's the 1st of June, and of course the Defence is not going to object on that. But the problem is the following: There is a stamp that was not translated, the stamp you have seen myself. It may be I may have lost my temper a bit, but this stamp clearly says that it's the military hospital of Dobrinja. On other documents that I wanted to show, we also have the documents that come from the same hospital which relate to similar problems. We also see stamps. On those stamps, there is no mention of a military hospital. So we suspect that it is not maybe necessarily the same hospital, or it is not maybe necessarily the same hospital we think we are talking about. And there is also another point which is very important. We were always told that there were numbers, protocol numbers, given. You will see, Mr. President, that in a document that I will show you like this from afar, because this is a document that we will submit to the Prosecution later on, we can see protocol numbers. They appear on these documents and they are all in chronological order. I read 5, 6, 7, and so on. However, in the lists that the Prosecution gave us, lists of names of wounded people during this event, the protocols do not follow in a chronological order, and the Defence does not understand how can it be that some documents that can be pertinent to this incident are presented in a chronological order in terms of the protocol numbers, whereas in other cases there is no chronological order, and then in the medical documents, that are the only documents that are given to us by the Prosecution, they completely disappear. We do not use terms such as "manipulations," but we must. We are forced to notice that there is not -- it's -- this information is not always concurrent. Some elements appear to be originals. Some documents seem to be originals because they were written by hand, and we gladly believe that this is the result of what had happened at the moment where these patients were examined, were treated. And later on, patients who were treated later on. But in the list that we have, we have also the ages of patients. And all of a sudden, in some of the lists that we obtained, the ages disappeared, whereas we see that most of these people were people who were either mobilised, or if they were not mobilised, they were mobilisable. They were in age to be drafted. So this is the reason for which - and I will finish here - this is the reason why the Defence requests once again that the Prosecution gives all the documents, the originals, all the originals of these medical documents, so that everybody in this Chamber and around this Chamber may be certain of the origin of the documents and the authenticity of the protocols. This is the request that we are formulating. I would have wanted to hand the documents right now. They will be handed to you later on. They might not have an immediate impact on the witness. You will know why, because this is a global, general issue. And you know why now the Defence is asking of your Chamber to render a decision which will help that the Prosecution bring all the originals of these documents, the protocols, the originals of these medical protocols that we are talking about. And we thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that apart from giving grounds for your objection, you also put a request to the Prosecution. Mr. Stamp, since it's already a quarter to 1.00, I'd rather have a break now, but of course I'll give you an opportunity to respond to -- unless you say I can do it in one minute or one minute and a half. But you'd rather not do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would prefer to take advantage of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then have a break until 5 minutes past 1.00. May I remind you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that the time used in cross-examination is already approximately the time used in examination-in-chief. This is not to stop you immediately, but the experience of the past taught me that I cannot leave it entirely in your hands. So please be aware that at a certain moment, I'll say that the time is over, after, of course, having consulted the other members of the Chamber. One other question for both parties: The Chamber is considering whether it would be good to ask the witness to provide the original of this document. I mean, if there is a better copy available, why not use it? So this is not a general rule on whether we would always have to obtain the originals. But if it's in this courtroom, this Chamber sees hardly any reason why not, since especially the witness consented to it, why not get the original. If the parties would have any observation in that respect, we would like to hear from them after the break. We'll have a break until 5 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I'll first give you the opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I took the opportunity at the break to have a look at the question raised by the Court and the submission by my learned friend, and I confess that I'm afraid that I cannot -- I do not understand the relevance of it to the issue of the admissibility of this document which, to my understanding, is what the Court asked about. In respect to the admissibility of this document, it is conceded that there are at least two areas which are not translated. That which the Defence thought was important, they, as they are entitled to, did cross-examine upon it and did have the witness read on to the record the words which were not translated. And notwithstanding that a stamp ought to have been translated, it is my submission that this does not sufficiently detract from the usefulness of the document for the Court to determine if the document is tendered, to establish, and again, I repeat, the cross-examination is not over. If there is any area of the document which the Defence feels ought to be translated to assist the Court in its determination, they could inquire of it and have it read into the record. I cannot address the Court on what my learned friend has said about other documents insofar as it might be relevant to the issue which the Court raised and asked about in respect of this document marked P2506B. Those documents are documents that are handed to the Defence by the Prosecution and which we propose at a later time to call witnesses about, and these witnesses are absolutely able to speak to the concerns of the Defence in respect of these documents. I certainly do not think that this witness, with regard to what his testimony has been so far, would be able to speak about any of the matters raised by learned friend, and certainly those matters raised were not responsive to the question asked by the Court. If it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, does this cause any additional observation from your side?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. President, I do not understand how it is so that my colleague didn't understand what I said. It is not only a problem with regards to translation, and we all understood this, but it was more of a general problem that I wished to raise. And at the end of this hearing, when the end of the cross-examination of this witness, I will try to establish this. Now I will ask some questions on some documents that are handed to the Prosecution and we will submit these documents to the witness shortly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll give our final decision on the admission into evidence of this document at the end of the examination of the witness but, at this moment, the Chamber sees no need to give a negative decision in respect of this document. Before resuming with the witness, I would have one or two -- perhaps first, a request for the parties. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I've seen that sometimes you ask the witness to read a certain part, or I do understand that you're going to ask the witness whether there's any number on a document. Couldn't the parties agree upon that? I mean, if both parties say that there's no number such as the number appearing at the end of the list on the document, we don't have to ask the witness to check and look at the back side as well. I mean, that's not something that is -- that's not an exercise that's better done by a witness than either by the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. parties or by the Court itself. So it would save us time, I think, if we would not ask witnesses to do, to establish, what is obvious to everyone what could be established by the parties easily themselves. Then before resuming, I still -- we have taken into consideration, Mr. Stamp, that you said that a decision on the 360-degrees photograph could be delayed. We understood it that you are still willing to assist Mr. Piletta-Zanin since the precise position of the 360-degrees photograph seems to bother him, to assist him and to help him in order to find out. At the same time, this Chamber thinks that a decision could be taken as far as the admissibility of the 360-degrees photograph is concerned. The reasons given by Mr. Piletta-Zanin not -- the additional reasons, apart from I would say the standard reasons, are that the -- that they have problems in accepting the answers of the witness where he testified that he would have been hit by 1500 shrapnels. That was the first one. And the second one was that -- let me just have a look. And that he was one and-a-half metres away from the point of impact of the explosive. We try to locate exactly where these answers were given. As far as the shrapnel is concerned, the witness has testified that there were thousands -- there might have been thousands of fragments of shrapnels. He did not testify that he was hit by these thousands, neither that he was hit by 1500. But it was Mr. Piletta-Zanin who, in misrepresenting the testimony of the witness, said this at the beginning of his cross-examination. But apart from that, and also apart from whether the witness testified one and a half metres - at least in the transcript it appears as his testimony that it was 3 and a half metres - but I'm not sure about whether you could deduce from the video a different thing, but we'll have to check that. But this is all not relevant because the 360-degree photograph has not its probative value primarily in order to give answers to these doubts of the Prosecution as far as the truthfulness or the correctness of the answers are concerned. It gives a static view. And to that extent, it differs from the video, it gives a static view on the surroundings. It gives a general impression on where buildings approximately were located in relation to the football pitch and, therefore, one couldn't say that the 360-degrees photograph is not relevant, neither could it be said that it has no probative value. And therefore under Rule 89(C), it can be admitted into evidence. The Chamber further noted that, as far as our recollection goes, that the matter of one and-a-half metres or would it have been 3 and-a-half metres have not been raised as such during cross-examination. The Chamber notes this because it's the -- if you are not satisfied by an answer of the witness, the first thing the party should do in order to create no misunderstandings is to cross-examine the witness on those answers. So therefore, the 360-degree photograph as shown to Mr. Fazlic is admitted into evidence. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think we could resume the cross-examination of the witness. May I remind you that for a witness who was 12 years old at the time when it happened, I'll not allow any cynical or aggressive approach. Could the usher please bring in the witness. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you know that your remarks are always welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziabdic, you had to wait for a few minutes longer. We apologise for that, but Mr. Piletta-Zanin will now resume his cross-examination. Please be seated. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us, to the best of your recollection, how many soldiers there were during this football match?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Soldiers in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just soldiers.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: You mean people registered as members of the army or soldiers on duty?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us whether at this football match you saw any people wearing military uniforms, and how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of them were in uniform, conditionally speaking, in uniform, whereas others - I'm talking about soldiers - the others were without uniform. But I know from personal knowledge that they were members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an indication on how many people with either whole or partly uniforms were there, and how many people were there who you knew were soldiers but were not recognisable as such at that moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe about a third to one-half, but less than half. Between one third to less than one-half. I don't know exactly. I can't remember the exact number of people who were in uniform of one kind or another and those without uniform. I can't remember exactly, but I'm talking about the number of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this includes both categories, those who were either wearing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with and without.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. And if the witness doesn't understand the question properly and if he asks for clarification, would you please give it to him next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do so gladly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the time of the incident, how many players were there on the pitch who were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many there were players in all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for your answer. Witness, are you aware of the existence of a restaurant called Sunca at Dobrinja, Sunca or "Sun"?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I know of the mini market, like grocery store, that before the war was called Sunca. I'm not aware of any restaurant by that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, Witness, whether at the time of the war there was a prison there or a special camp?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, I'm going to show you some documents now. I'll begin with a document with the number D87. I think that's the right number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, please. Let me explain that the Prosecution has already received this document. Mr. President, I'm distributing it in the condition in which we have received it, so I'll make no comment as to the clarity or the legibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you have this document before you?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I see it, but not clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Do you recognise among the names to the left people that you may know?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, Aganspahic Rusmir, I know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell me in what line that person appears, so that we can all find him.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: From the number to the far right, 0026-7853, the first name after that. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, quite. But I don't know -- yes, quite. But I don't know if everyone has seen it. Witness, opposite that number, would you read what is found next to the number 17.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Sex: Male.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. What I wanted was before the three letters, G-O-D. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It means years, age. Age: 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. So that means that this person was 17 when he was wounded. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Another list will come soon but let us continue with this same name. Further up, we have another number on the far right. Could you read it out for us, please. If I read it, 1633, is that what you are seeing? Or maybe 1638?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: You mean the name above this one, 16 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, sorry. 1639 is the number I'm reading. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: You mean this number?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. That's right.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the number? Let us try it differently. Witness, the initials BR --

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: It is very unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. The initials BR, does that mean "number"?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes, number. Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Probably it means number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now, please, go on to Document D88, which the usher will be kind enough to give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to outline again that the Prosecution has been handed these documents, and they come from the Prosecution anyway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know the person whose name appears on this document? Or rather, the name has been struck, to the left, on top.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I find it very difficult to read this. I think I can only read the name, and the name of the parent. First name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. Could you read the date, the two dates that we see, and confirm whether it is the 12th of July, 1993, and the 17th of July, 1993? Are those two dates correct as I am reading them?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1993 is quite clear to me. And this is probably the 12th of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Would you now read what we see very clearly on the stamp, which is on the left-hand side of the signature of the doctor, and that is Dr. Dajir, I think. Could you read what you see on that stamp?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: "General Hospital, Sarajevo." "General Hospital, Sarajevo," and in the middle, it says "Dobrinja" with "P.O." That's what I see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. I shall now show you another document. We will soon come to the end of this exercise. It is number 89. And after that, we will also need number 90, so if it could be given to the usher as well. Witness, you have in front of you a piece of paper which is mostly in handwriting, and we can read "mortus ad latus" on it. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please read the fifth line in the centre of the left part of the document, the name of Mr. Damir Trebo.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you see on this document a number on the left-hand side, number 1739, next to the name of Mr. Trebo Damir?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know this gentleman, Mr. Damir Trebo?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One more document, please, for the witness.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Not by name. But I know the one under him. He was my friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] D90. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the fourth name from the bottom of that document? Does it have the same references?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: From the bottom. Trebo Damir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, quite. Quite. From the bottom of the page. You find the particulars of this gentleman, Mr. Damir Trebo?

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please, take your time.

utterances.speaker: Omer Hadziabdic
utterances.text: Yes. I see both the documents very clearly now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking only about this second document that you have just received. Will you please read what you find next to the abbreviation for number that is "Br" in Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to confer with my colleague, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Stamp, is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have no re-examination, if it pleases you. Maybe one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Having thought about it, no questions. I was going to ask him if he was the author of these documents, but I don't think it is necessary. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hadziabdic, we saw that you brought a document, and I think you said in between that this was the original of the document that has been shown to you and which has number P2506B on it. Did you compare the two documents, the one you brought and the one presented to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did superficially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you see any differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please, Madam Registrar, if the P2506B would be available, would it please be given to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing, except for this number here, 0067-887, and where the stamp is, it's unclear. You can't see the surgeon --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the original more clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Much clearer. Much clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, I asked you before, but the Court would perhaps, especially because you said the stamp is much clearer on the original you've brought, the Court would very much like to keep the copy you brought with you for the record of the Court. I don't know whether you need any receipt for that or whether you would like to have another copy made which indicates that the copy we provided you then with is a true copy of the original you gave us. If you are in need of that, please let us know or let those of the Victims and Witness Unit know so that we could prepare a copy for you if you would like to keep one. Mr. Usher -- but, let me just first ask you whether you need a copy to take home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I might perhaps need it in my life, so I'm willing to give the Court the original, but you provide me with a certified copy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll provide you with a certified copy. Would you then please give the -- both the original and the copy provided to you, P2506B, to the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could we please have a look at the document brought by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do any of the parties wish to inspect the document just given by the witness? Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we would like that very much, Mr. President, and thank you in advance. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have not, of course not, pre-numbered the evidence, and the Chamber is not sure whether what kind of character should be attached to it. So the copy of the -- the copy the witness brought, which seems to be exactly the same as P Exhibit 2506B is on the order of the Court admitted into evidence. And the number will be communicated to the parties at a later stage. Before, and not after, I've asked the booth whether we could deal with the documents for perhaps a couple minutes after the witness left the courtroom. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. I would like to ask the usher to guide the witness out of the courtroom, but I first would like to thank you very much for coming, Mr. Hadziabdic. It's a long way for you, I'm aware of that. We are also aware that the events you testified about happened when you were still a very young boy, and I also can imagine that the circumstances under which you have grown up might have influenced your life. We are aware of that, and I hope that you understand that the answers you've given to the questions of the parties and the questions of the Bench are important for us because we have to take decisions, and the information given by those who were present during these days and at that places are very much assisting us. So I would like to thank you very much and wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'll take care that you'll receive a certified copy as soon -- may I ask, Madam Registrar, to take care, because I expect that the witness will leave the Netherlands soon, that a certified copy will be made immediately so that he can perhaps through the Victims and Witness Unit be provided with a certified copy of the document.
